newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Shipley wants country put before airlines.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Shipley wants country put before airlines.

text.p: Transport Minister Jenny Shipley has urged the Australian government to put economic benefits ahead of individual airlines' interests in the debate over airlines' access to "beyond rights".

"There is no doubt in Australia that there is some tension between airlines' interests and Australia's interest," Shipley told journalists on Tuesday at a briefing on her recent discussions with Australian Transport Minister John Sharp.

"The vast majority of our presentation and items were built around the fact that it is actually in the economy, the public interest to try and expand both access and capacity into our respective countries than worry about the fate of any particular airline."
She said Sharp had been receptive and had agreed to confront airlines with the economic arguments.
"The problem is you have got two airlines in Australia who you could argue are -- the phrase was used in Australia by a person who will remain nameless -- a comfortable duopoly.

"We need as many destinations and access as we can and if the planes start off at 45 percent (loading) and over a five year period grow to a credible capacity carriage then from the country's point of view those are the goals we should be pursuing, whereas carriers often have an incentive to only have one flight a week or two flights a week in the hope it will be full."
She said it was not so much a conflict as New Zealand taking the medium term view.
"And I think trying to get the medium term base developed is what we need to convince the (Australian) ministers of."
She said the goals of a single aviation market and a commercial alliance between Air New Zealand and Ansett had been achieved and it was now time "for serious conversation on beyond rights".
Shipley said airlines sometimes argued they wanted to fill planes before they expanded capacity and routes, in some emerging markets it might be crucial to be there first.

"We tried to prevail on the Australians ... It is quite inappropriate we do anything that might allow the Australasian airlines to languish in the view that they don't have to be absolutely competitive.
"I felt anxious that New Zealand was left having to put a continued and major case for the overall benefits for New Zealand and Australia by economic growth."
Asked if she would move to appeal directly to consumers in Australia she said: "Come and ask me in six months if we are no further forward."
She said it was unclear whether existing arrangement would allow New Zealand and Austrlaia to meet their ambitious targets for tourism growth.
Shipley will meet Sharp next in Cairns in May.
Speaking at a news conference in New Zealand on Monday Australian Prime Minister John Howard said there was no timetable for a decision.
"The beyond rights issue is very important to New Zealand, I've understood that since the beginning," Howard said.
"I think it's fair to say that it's always been seen by us as having a degree of difficulty which is greater than the original negotiations involving the single aviation market."
He said he was happy to see the discussions continuing but would give no time frame for when a decision would be made on beyond rights.
Existing arrangements allow Air New Zealand to fly the equivalent of 12 wide-bodied planes out of Australia to North America and Asian markets.
The rights were included in the initial agreement for a single aviation market unilaterally cancelled by former Australian prime minister Paul Keating.
